**Result:** Every input except #7 gets the same button under all the assignments that fit. #7 is a coin flip between green and red, and I chose green.

## Identifying the features (Y)

- **Y4 = bit 4.** In X1-Y4-Z3, blue appears exactly when bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y2 = bit 1.** In X6-Y2-Z1, green appears exactly when bit 1 is 0 in both stimuli.
- **Y3 = bit 2.** In X5-Y3-Z4, yellow appears exactly when bit 2 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y1 = bit 3.** In X2-Y1-Z1, bits 2 and 4 each fail on at least one example, and bit 3 fits all of them.

## Rules and buttons (X and Z)

The examples allow two global readings, A and B.

| Component | Reading A | Reading B |
|---|---|---|
| Z1 | green = true, red = false | red = true, green = false |
| X2 | both are the same | exactly one is 1 |
| X6 | neither is 1 | at least one is 1 |
| X3 (Z2: yellow = same) | exactly one is 1 | both are the same |

Under both readings, X5 and X1 are "both are 1" and "not both are 1", one each, in either order. Z3 and Z4 follow from that choice.

So there are 4 fitting assignments, and they give only two different predictions for the new task X5-Y2-Z1:

- **(A, X5 = both)** or **(B, X5 = not both):** green when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli, otherwise red.
- **(A, X5 = not both)** or **(B, X5 = both):** red when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli, otherwise green.

Only input #7 (1100 1000) has bit 1 equal to 1 in both stimuli. The four assignments agree on the other 15 inputs, but those 15 flip with the choice between the two predictions: they are red under the first and green under the second. So the choice decides all 16 answers, not just #7.

## Choosing between the two predictions

No cross-component pattern settles this. I lean slightly toward the reading where Z1's "true" button is green and X5 is the positive rule "both are 1". On that reading the new task is green only when both stimuli have bit 1 equal to 1.

## Predictions

| # | Input | Bit 1 values | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 1100 1000 | 1, 1 | green |
| 1–6, 8–16 | (all others) | not both 1 | red |

The examples do not determine the answers uniquely. My confidence is about 0.55, because everything rests on one guess between two equally consistent options.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: red, yellow, green, or blue. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> green` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is green.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
